<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B controlled the decisive clash points more effectively. B's opening cleanly identified three live tensions (detectability, the "no exchange rate" problem, and superior alternative remedies), and its Pressure Questions forced A into a genuine bind: A's answer to the grocery hypothetical ("condition it") never actually resolved what parity requires when price gains and labor harm conflict, which B correctly flagged as a retreat from "parity" to mere "counting." That extracted concession—that labor harm can never by itself veto a demonstrated price benefit under A's own operationalization—was never squarely repaired by A in Rebuttal 2 or Closing. B also landed a sharp, underrebutted point in Rebuttal 2 (A4/B4 exchange): A's flagship example, the one-hospital town, is already a monopoly on the output side and thus already caught by existing price-side merger review, undercutting the central motivating case for the motion. A's Closing did not directly answer this, leaving one of the most damaging blows on the table. A's rebuttals (SSNIP-style wage test analogy, remedy-timing argument) were solid and prevented an outright blowout, but B's arguments were more precise, better used the Pressure Questions round to reshape the debate, and gave a cleaner, more decidable account of why full parity is unworkable while "counting" preserves the core protective function without the undefined exchange-rate problem.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (A2 answer): pointing out that a merger creating a single buyer of labor in a one-hospital town also creates a single seller of hospital care, meaning the scenario is already caught by existing price-side merger review — directly undercutting A's central illustrative example, a point A never adequately answered in the Closing.</best_rebuttal>
